Tech

NVIDIA co-develops new sports products to help grow market

By Joe Lemire
10.05.2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 2:50
Instaread

NVIDIA is advancing its reach into the sports industry after recently debuting a series of new media and technology products at the IBC conference in Amsterdam.

Among the new features shared by the leading maker of advanced GPUs for processing video and artificial intelligence were:

  • 3D Body Pose: A tool to estimate athletes’ 3D movement from a single camera
  • Video Frame Generation: The use of AI to create new, intermediary frames to retroactively create slow-motion replays
  • TrueHDR: The ability to enhance standard video into high-dynamic range (HDR) quality for richer viewing

While NVIDIA is not the seller of these products, it co-develops use cases in order to help seed the market. Jamie Allan -- NVIDIA’s director of AI for Sports, AdTech & Enterprise Media -- shared that some of its collaborators include Hawk-Eye, Stats Perform, Peripheral Labs and Skyrim.ai.

“Every industry is finding new and exciting ways to leverage the evolution of artificial intelligence through new ways to apply perception AI, generative AI, now agentic AI and physical AI across their spaces,” Allan told SBJ. “In sports, all of those areas are applicable, which makes it a really interesting space to go and see how can we help accelerate those needs that developers, that leagues, federations, broadcasters are looking to achieve.”

NVIDIA’s goal, he added, is what he described as foundational problem solving: taking a hard problem whose solution would have broad applications and solving for that. Allan gave the example that its 3D Body Pose product -- which does exist commercially from SkillCorner, Teamworks’ Sportlogiq and others -- has its roots in self-driving cars.

“The advancements we’ve been doing around body pose estimation, which is obviously important to sports for many different reasons, the R&D process for us to advance that actually started around autonomous vehicles and physical AI to advance how computers understand the real world to make autonomous driving safer,” Allan said.

Some of the new media offerings, which are left up to broadcasts to implement, could help enrich the viewing experience, both visually and via storytelling, given the growing interest in advanced data.

NVIDIA -- the world’s most valuable company with a market cap exceeding $5.5T -- has its influence on the entire process “from grass to screen,” as Allan put it, including the image quality and the specially trained AI models that can surface insights for fan consumption and engagement.

“The data about a game or a sport or a team is very specific,” he said. “So how can we go and take that knowledge that we learn from the industry, turn it into a recipe of sorts that we can then give back to developers to say, ‘If you want to really quickly adapt a cost-effective open-source model for your sport, here’s the best way to do it.’”
